title: OpenAI Has a Special Email for Employees to Flag Problems Directly to Leadership
excerpt: The company's internal "Friction" email gives staff a direct channel to report workplace bottlenecks — and the messages can land in Sam Altman's inbox.
body:
• OpenAI maintains a special internal email address called "Friction" that employees can use to report workplace problems and bottlenecks directly to leadership.
  • Messages sent to the Friction email can reach CEO Sam Altman, who has been known to act on them personally.
  • The system reflects OpenAI's attempt to maintain startup-like responsiveness as it has scaled from roughly 1,000 to over 3,000 employees in the past two years.
  • The mechanism stands out in an industry where rapid growth often creates layers of bureaucracy that slow internal communication.

At most technology companies, an employee with a workplace complaint has a familiar set of options: file an HR ticket, message a manager on Slack, or vent to colleagues over coffee. At OpenAI, there is another path — a dedicated email address called "Friction" that routes workplace problems directly to senior leadership, and in some cases, straight to CEO Sam Altman.

The internal channel, first detailed by Fortune, gives employees across the company a way to flag issues that are slowing them down — from bureaucratic delays and cross-team coordination failures to resource constraints and process breakdowns. The name itself is telling: rather than burying complaints in a helpdesk queue, the system is designed to surface the specific points of organizational friction that drag on productivity.

How the Friction Email Works

When an employee identifies a bottleneck or systemic issue that conventional channels haven't resolved, they can email the Friction address with a description of the problem. The message is routed to leadership, where it is triaged and, in many cases, acted on quickly. Altman has reportedly taken a personal interest in the process, sometimes intervening directly when an employee raises a concern that points to a deeper organizational problem.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=OHTOKYtdE-Q

The approach aligns with what former employees have described as OpenAI's unusually flat and fast-moving internal culture. The company runs almost entirely on Slack rather than traditional email, and engineers are expected to take initiative without waiting for formal approvals. The Friction email adds a safety valve for situations where that speed breaks down — a mechanism to short-circuit bureaucratic gridlock before it compounds.

"I believe there are a few important new things the world will need to get right as we enter this next period."

— Brad Lightcap, former OpenAI COO, on the challenges of scaling the company

Scaling Pains at a Hypergrowth Company

The Friction email exists in the context of extraordinary organizational growth. OpenAI has expanded from roughly 1,000 employees to more than 3,000 in the span of a year, a pace that has strained internal processes. Former engineer Calvin French-Owen, who left the company in 2025, described the challenges of that expansion: reporting lines changed frequently, multiple teams often built duplicate tools, and the sheer velocity of product development left little time for organizational refinement.

For a company building what it believes may be the most transformative technology in history, the cost of internal friction is not just lost productivity — it is lost time in a race with well-funded competitors including Anthropic and Google DeepMind. The Friction email is one way OpenAI has tried to keep the feedback loop between frontline employees and decision-makers as short as possible.

An Unusual Approach in Tech

Direct-to-CEO escalation channels are rare in Silicon Valley, where most large companies rely on structured management hierarchies and formal feedback processes. Some companies have anonymous hotlines or suggestion boxes, but few offer employees a named, sanctioned path to flag operational issues with the expectation that the CEO may personally respond.

The system does carry risks. An open channel to leadership can create information overload, and employees may hesitate to use it if they fear being seen as complainers. But at a company where speed and execution are existential priorities, the trade-off appears to lean in favor of surfacing problems quickly — even if that means the CEO's inbox gets a bit noisier.

OpenAI has not publicly commented on the specifics of how the Friction email operates or how frequently it is used.
